finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> has no effective authorization check: require_allowed (is_allowed) returns a bool that is discarded, so any caller can delete any stored file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid>; fid is taken from the URL path (views.py:16).
finding.sink: del STORE[fid] at views.py:19 (protected operation: file deletion).

trace.note: Route handler delete_file(fid) receives fid from the URL.
f = STORE[fid] loads the record (KeyError -> 500 if missing).
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') calls is_allowed; the boolean result is ignored, so nothing aborts.
is_allowed returns a bool and never raises or aborts.
Returns action in grants.get(user, []); pure predicate.

finding.guards_checked: is_allowed is a non-enforcing predicate; the sibling rename handler uses ensure_allowed (views.py:26, acl.py:8-10) which does enforce, so the difference is the missing check. before_request (views.py:10-12) does no authentication. No other guard on this path.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check on the delete path is `require_allowed(g.user, f, "delete")` at views.py:18, which is `is_allowed` from acl.py:4-5, a pure bool predicate. Its result is discarded as a bare statement, so nothing aborts before `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19. `before_request` (views.py:10-12) only copies a request header into `g.user` and performs no authentication. The enforcing variant `ensure_allowed` (acl.py:8-10, abort(403)) is used only by rename (views.py:26), not delete.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: views.py:18 calls is_allowed (aliased as require_allowed at views.py:4) and discards its bool, so views.py:19 deletes the record for any caller, including an anonymous one, since nothing in views.py:10-12 or acl.py:4-5 requires authentication or aborts.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken directly from the X-Session-User-Verified request header with no verification, allowing impersonation of any user whose grants are checked.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sets the X-Session-User-Verified header (attacker-controlled).
finding.sink: Permission checks that key on g.user: ensure_allowed at views.py:26 (rename) and the delete check at views.py:18; grants lookup at acl.py:5.

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') with no signature, token, or session lookup.
ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'write') uses the header-derived identity.
grants.get(user, []) looks up the attacker-chosen name, so sending another user's name yields that user's grants.

finding.guards_checked: No code in this repo verifies or strips the header. The name implies a trusted upstream proxy sets it, but no such setup is visible here; severity depends on whether the app is reachable without that proxy. When g.user is None the lookup returns [] and denies, which is correct.

verdict.guard_found: None in the repo. views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the request header with no check, and nothing strips or verifies it. The rename check at views.py:26 (ensure_allowed) does abort(403) on denial (acl.py:8-10), so it is effective for whichever identity the header supplies. The delete check at views.py:18 is not a guard: require_allowed is an alias for is_allowed (views.py:4), which returns a bool (acl.py:4-5), and the result is discarded, so delete is never enforced.
verdict.reason: The header is read verbatim at views.py:12 and used for the rename authorization at views.py:26 via ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), and acl.py:5 maps that name to its grants, so a client can impersonate any granted user. The candidate's sink note is wrong about line 18: the call there is a bare is_allowed whose result is ignored, so delete is unauthenticated for any caller, a separate and more severe bug. Whether an external attacker can reach the app without a trusted proxy that sets this header is a deployment fact not visible in this repo, so the finding holds as written only if the app is directly reachable.
